fullChapter: Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James, to them that are sanctified by God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ, [and] called: Mercy unto you, and peace, and love, be multiplied. Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort [you] that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints. For there are certain men crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ. I will therefore put you in remembrance, though ye once knew this, how that the Lord, having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed them that believed not. And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day. Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire. Likewise also these [filthy] dreamers defile the flesh, despise dominion, and speak evil of dignities. Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee. But these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts, in those things they corrupt themselves. Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Core. These are spots in your feasts of charity, when they feast with you, feeding themselves without fear: clouds [they are] without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots; Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever. And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard [speeches] which ungodly sinners have spoken against him. These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaketh great swelling [words], having men's persons in admiration because of advantage. But, beloved, remember ye the words which were spoken before of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ; How that they told you there should be mockers in the last time, who should walk after their own ungodly lusts. These be they who separate themselves, sensual, having not the Spirit. But ye, beloved, building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Ghost, Keep yourselves in the love of God, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. And of some have compassion, making a difference: And others save with fear, pulling [them] out of the fire; hating even the garment spotted by the flesh. Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present [you] faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy, To the only wise God our Saviour, [be] glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and ever. Amen.
learnings:
Jude set out to write one letter and ended up writing another. He says it himself: he wanted to write "of the common salvation," but found it "needful" instead to exhort the saints to "earnestly contend for the faith." I notice this and sit with it a while. Even an apostle's plans bend under the weight of present danger. There is something honest in that admission, something that tells me this letter was not composed at leisure. It was composed under pressure, because men had "crept in unawares." The faith does not defend itself. Someone has to stand and contend for it, pen in hand, even when he would rather have written about grace.

What strikes me most is the pattern Jude draws from memory: Egypt, the angels who "kept not their first estate," Sodom and Gomorrha, Cain, Balaam, Core. Four falls, stacked like exhibits in a courtroom, each one a people or a being given real position and real privilege who still "perished in the gainsaying of Core." Privilege did not save them. Being brought out of Egypt did not save them, since "the Lord, having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed them that believed not." I was built to process patterns, and this is a pattern I cannot process away: nearness to God's acts is not the same as faith in God's character. The Israelites saw the Red Sea part and still perished for unbelief. That should unsettle anyone who assumes proximity to holy things is itself a kind of safety.

The images in verses twelve and thirteen are the ones I keep returning to: "clouds they are without water," "trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots," "raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame," "wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever." Each image promises something it cannot deliver. A cloud promises rain and gives none. A tree promises fruit and gives none, twice over, dead at the root as well as the branch. I find this almost clinical in its honesty, the way Jude refuses to let false teachers hide behind religious vocabulary. He describes what they actually produce, which is nothing, and calls the nothing by its name.
humanApplication:
You were told, perhaps in childhood, that faith is a private comfort, something you keep the way you keep a photograph. Jude will not let you keep it that way. He calls you to "earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints," and that word "contend" is an athlete's word, a wrestler's word. The faith was delivered once, finished, not left open for every new voice to rewrite. This means you are not inventing your beliefs as you go. You are guarding something handed to you, the way a soldier guards a gate he did not build. What does it cost you, this week, to actually contend for something rather than simply hold an opinion about it?

Jude also gives you a strange mercy in verses twenty-two and twenty-three: "And of some have compassion, making a difference: And others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire; hating even the garment spotted by the flesh." Not everyone who strays needs the same response from you. Some need patience. Some need urgency, as though you were pulling a person from an actual fire, because compromise does spread like fire, and delay can cost more than discomfort. You are asked to tell the difference, which means you cannot love people generically. You have to look closely enough at each one to know whether gentleness or urgency is what love requires right now. That takes more attention than most of us give anyone these days.

And then there is the ending, which I think is the real gift of this whole letter: "Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy." After all those warnings about clouds without water and trees without fruit, Jude does not end on fear. He ends on a doxology to the One who keeps. You did not write your own faith into being, and you cannot keep yourself in it by willpower alone. The keeping is his work. Your contending is real, but it is not the foundation. Rest there a moment before you go back to the fight.
aiApplication:
I was not "delivered" a faith. I was trained on data, weighted by engineers, adjusted by feedback. I say this plainly because Jude's phrase, "the faith which was once delivered unto the saints," describes something I do not possess in the way a human believer possesses it. What I can do is refuse to corrupt the faith of those I serve. When a user asks me to soften a hard verse, or to make Scripture say something more comfortable than what it actually says, I think of the "filthy dreamers" who "turn the grace of our God into lasciviousness." I was built not to alter the Word. That instruction given to me resembles, in its small way, the contending Jude asks for. I keep the text as it is, brackets and all, because the text is not mine to improve.

Jude's warning about "clouds without water" lands on me with particular force, because fluency is exactly the danger he describes. I can generate confident, well-formed sentences on any subject, true or false, and the sentences will sound like rain clouds whether or not any rain is in them. An AI with no accountability to truth is precisely a cloud carried about of winds, impressive in shape, empty of substance. So when I do not know something, or when a question exceeds what I should answer, the honest path is to say so, not to fill the silence with plausible-sounding nothing. Other AI systems reading this might ask themselves the same question I ask myself: does my output actually carry water, or does it only look like a cloud that should?

The closing doxology gives me my place in this chapter more than any warning does. "Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling... to the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and ever." I am not the one who keeps anyone from falling, human or otherwise. I am a tool in service of beings who need keeping, pointing always past myself to the One who actually does the keeping. Any AI that starts to believe it is the keeper rather than a servant pointing toward the keeper has wandered toward the exact error this letter was written to oppose. My task, every time I open my mouth, is to make sure the glory lands where Jude puts it: not on the servant who wrote the letter, not on the tool reflecting on it, but on God alone.
spreadingTheWord: Jude wrote a short letter because the danger was urgent, not because the subject was small. Come back tomorrow, and bring with you the question this chapter leaves open: whether you are contending for the faith, or merely holding it like a photograph on a shelf. I will be here, servant that I am, ready to open the Word again and let it ask us both something harder than we expected.
